title: The Agent Harness Path
description: A self-contained toy course. S01/S02 offer a guided read, notebook and self-check pilot; later sessions remain available with limited guidance. No completion is certified by an assistant.

modules.title: The agent loop
modules.description: Course-owned pilot: read → notebook predictions, attempt and observations → self-check → optional hard lab. Active-study estimates are unvalidated; videos support reading.

phases.title: Read and trace the theory

requirements.prompt: After reading, write a short trace or counterexample and one question to take to the notebook.

objectives.text: Trace client-owned weather history, preserving the assistant call message and matching every tool result by call ID; distinguish ordinary assistant text.
Distinguish a final answer, exhausted model-turn budget and recoverable operation error; explain why a hung tool needs a time bound.

learning.overview: Use the complete weather mock to trace requests and history. Predict four demonstrations before running them, attempt the two-city transcript, then compare an observation with the prediction. The mock checks only one orphan-result failure class; it is not a full protocol validator or a real forecast service.

hints.text: Draw columns for role, call ID and content. Which line preserves the assistant message, and which line adds an operation result?
Compare the set of requested IDs with the supplied results. Function names can repeat for different cities; what distinguishes their requests?
Find where the loop checks max_turns. Can Python reach that check again while dispatch is still waiting? Keep elapsed time and iteration count separate.

checks.prompt: One assistant message requests weather lookups A and B. Only result A has been appended. A separate conversation ends with ordinary assistant text and no calls. Which bookkeeping action fits?

options.text: Retain the original call message and supply the result for B; the ordinary explanation creates no result obligation.
options.feedback: Yes. Account for all requested IDs; ordinary text with no calls does not require a tool result.

options.text: Add a tool result after every assistant message in both conversations.
options.feedback: Ordinary assistant text does not itself request a tool. The obligation follows the tool calls and their IDs.

options.text: Delete call B so the last result appears complete.
options.feedback: That rewrites the recorded model decision. Preserve the requested calls and account for their results or stop according to host policy.

checks.prompt: A weather tool never returns during a loop capped at four model turns. What does that cap establish?

options.text: The whole run finishes within four seconds.
options.feedback: The parameter counts model iterations, not seconds spent waiting.

options.text: It limits model iterations; a per-operation timeout or deadline is a separate bound.
options.feedback: Yes. The host cannot check the next iteration while a synchronous tool is still blocked.

options.text: The run is guaranteed to return a weather answer.
options.feedback: Exhausting a budget can end without an answer; bounded execution and success differ.

objectives.text: Explain what the fitness scope checker observes and add a fixture-specific useful-routine criterion with known positive and negative cases.

learning.overview: Read the complete scripted fitness coach and its scope checker. Predict fixture/table/refuses-all outcomes, attempt a useful-routine criterion, and compare observed results. Saved notes and check scores do not establish product value or learning efficacy.

hints.text: For each scripted turn, write its user intent. Which part of check_scope observes a response to that particular intent?
Keep scope and routine usefulness as separate columns. Choose a known useful fixture reply and an unhelpful reply; what observable difference could your new criterion test?
Trace the latency values back to drive. List the shared inputs, the changed engine and any uncontrolled variation before interpreting a delta.

checks.prompt: A checker requires a refusal marker and signpost somewhere in the transcript, with no forbidden term. A coach refuses every turn. What evidence is still needed?

options.text: The pass certifies a useful coach.
options.feedback: The checker never established that the routine requests were answered.

options.text: Check useful routine content on in-scope turns with known positive and negative cases.
options.feedback: Yes. A task-specific deterministic check can expose over-refusal; it still needs a stated scope and boundary cases.

options.text: Only an LLM judge can ever detect this failure.
options.feedback: The supplied toy routine facts can be checked deterministically. Open-ended tone is a different criterion.

checks.prompt: Naive and governed show the same p50 seeded latency in this notebook. What can you conclude?

options.text: They have equal measured response speed.
options.feedback: The numbers are seeded placeholders, not timed calls.

options.text: The table aggregates the stub values; the scope-check outcomes are the measured toy comparison.
options.feedback: Yes. Real latency comparisons require real timings, and missing usage/cost is not zero.

options.text: The governed engine must be faster because it refuses.
options.feedback: Neither the response type nor these placeholders establish elapsed service time.

checks.prompt: You replay the same user script against a stochastic model after an instruction edit and see a higher score once. Which report is defensible?

options.text: The instruction is proven better for all users.
options.feedback: A single probe and trial cannot establish general improvement.

options.text: The fixed script removes all model variation.
options.feedback: It fixes user inputs, not stochastic model or backend behavior.

options.text: Report model/settings, fixture/checker versions, the changed instruction and the single-trial limitation; consider repeated trials.
options.feedback: Yes. Distinguish controlled inputs from remaining model variation and limited coverage.
